entries.definition: Having the nature of a bean; like a bean.
One of the small sesamoid bones situated behind the condyles ofthe femur, in some mammals.

Of, pertaining to, or in the manner of, the Roman general,Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus; cautious; dilatory; avoiding adecisive contest. Fabian policy, a policy like that of FabiusMaximus, who, by carefully avoiding decisive contests, foiledHannibal, harassing his army by marches, countermarches, andambuscades; a policy of delays and cautions.

To compose fables; hence, to write or speak fiction ; to writeor utter what is not true. "He Fables not." Shak.Vain now the tales which fabling poets tell. Prior.He fables, yet speaks truth. M. Arnold.
A writer of fables; a fabulist; a dealer in untruths orfalsehoods. Br. Hall.
One of the metrical tales of the Trouvères, or early poets ofthe north of France.
To frame; to built; to construct. [Obs.] "Fabric theirmansions." J. Philips.
One who fabricates; a manufacturer. Simmonds.
One who fabricates; one who constructs or makes.The fabricator of the works of Ossian. Mason.
A woman who fabricates.
Pertaining to a workman, or to work in stone, metal, wood etc.;as, fabrile skill.
One who invents or writes fables.
To invent, compose, or relate fables or fictions. G. S. Faber.
A large ornamental letter used, esp. by the early printers, atthe commencement of the chapters and other divisions of a book.Brande & C.
The front of a building; esp., the principal front, having somearchitectural pretensions. Thus a church is said to have its facadeunfinished, though the interior may be in use.
Ten degrees in extent of a sign of the zodiac. Chaucer.
Having (such) a face, or (so many) faces; as, smooth-faced,two-faced.
A smooth circumscribed surface; as, the articular facet of abone.

Facetious; witty; humorous. [Archaic] "A facete discourse."Jer. Taylor."How to interpose" with a small, smart remark, sentiment facete, orunctuous anecdote. Prof. Wilson.-- Fa*cete"ly, adv.-- Fa*cete"ness, n.
Having facets.
Witty or humorous writings or saying; witticisms; merryconceits.
See Facet, n.
The material of the outside or front side, as of a wall orbuilding; facing.
See Fascia.

Of or pertaining to the face; as, the facial artery, vein, ornerve.-- Fa"cial*ly, adv. Facial angle (Anat.), the angle, in a skull,included between a straight line (ab, in the illustrations), from themost prominent part of the forehead to the front efge of the upperjaw bone, and another (cd) from this point to the center of theexternal auditory opening. See Gnathic index, under Gnathic.
The multiplicand. See Facient,
The general aspect or habit of a species, or group of species,esp. with reference to its adaptation to its environment.

To make easy or less difficult; to free from difficulty orimpediment; to lessen the labor of; as, to facilitate the executionof a task.To invite and facilitate that line of proceeding which the times callfor. I. Taylor.
The act of facilitating or making easy.
The finishing of any face of a wall with material differentfrom that of which it is chiefly composed, or the coating or materialso used.
In a facing manner or position.
Atrociously wicked. [Obs.] Jer. Taylor.-- Fa*cin"o*rous*ness, n. [Obs.]
Speech; eloquence. [Obs.]Her facound eke full womanly and plain. Chaucer.

A copy of anything made, either so as to be deceptive or so asto give every part and detail of the original; an exact copy orlikeness. Facsimile telegraph, a telegraphic apparatus reproducingmessages in autograph.
One of the divisions or parties of charioteers (distinguishedby their colors) in the games of the circus.
Belonging to a faction; being a partisan; taking sides. [Obs.]Always factionary on the party of your general. Shak.
One of a faction. Abp. Bancroft.
One who promotes faction.

Made by art, in distinction from what is produced by nature;artificial; sham; formed by, or adapted to, an artificial orconventional, in distinction from a natural, standard or rule; notnatural; as, factitious cinnabar or jewels; a factitious taste.-- Fac-ti"tious*ly, adv.-- Fac*ti"tious-ness, n.He acquires a factitious propensity, he forms an incorrigible habit,of desultory reading. De Quincey.

Pertaining to that relation which is proper when the act, as ofa transitive verb, is not merely received by an object, but producessome change in the object, as when we say, He made the water wine.Sometimes the idea of activity in a verb or adjective involves in ita reference to an effect, in the way of causality, in the activevoice on the immediate objects, and in the passive voice on thesubject of such activity. This second object is called the factitiveobject. J. W. Gibbs.
Making; having power to make. [Obs.] "You are . . . factive,not destructive." Bacon.
In fact; by the act or fact. De facto. (Law) See De facto.

One who transacts business for another; an agent; a substitute;especially, a mercantile agent who buys and sells goods and transactsbusiness for others in commission; a commission merchant orconsignee. He may be a home factor or a foreign factor. He may buyand sell in his own name, and he is intrusted with the possession andcontrol of the goods; and in these respects he differs from a broker.Story. Wharton.My factor sends me word, a merchant's fled That owes me for a hundredtun of wine. Marlowe.
The allowance given to a factor, as a compensation for hisservices; -- called also a commission.
A factor who is a woman. [R.]
Related to factorials.
The act of resolving into factors.
The business of a factor.
A person employed to do all kinds of work or business. B.Jonson.
Relating to, or containing, facts. [R.]
A man's own act and deed; particularly:(a) (Civil Law) Anything stated and made certain.(b) (Testamentary Law) The due execution of a will, includingeverything necessary to its validity.
An invoice or bill of parcels.

Groups of small shining spots on the surface of the sun whichare brighter than the other parts of the photosphere. They aregenerally seen in the neighborhood of the dark spots, and aresupposed to be elevated portions of the photosphere. Newcomb.
Of or pertaining to the faculæ. R. A. Proctor.
Having the power to live under different conditions; as, afacultative parasite, a plant which is normally saprophytic, butwhich may exist wholly or in part as a parasite; -- opposed toobligate.

The body of person to whom are intrusted the government andinstruction of a college or university, or of one of its departments;the president, professors, and tutors in a college. Dean of faculty.See under Dean.-- Faculty of advocates. (Scot.) See under Advocate.
Eloquent. [Archaic]
Eloquement; full of words. [Archaic]
Eloquence; readiness of speech. [Archaic]
A hobby ; freak; whim.-- Fad"dist, n.It is your favorite fad to draw plans. G. Eliot.
A vapid or meaningless remark; a commonplace; nonsense.
To trifle; to toy.-- v. t.
Weak; insipid; tasteless; commonplace. [R.] "Passages that aresomewhat fade." Jeffrey.His masculine taste gave him a sense of something fade and ludicrous.De Quincey.
That has lost freshness, color, or brightness; grown dim. "Hisfaded cheek." Milton.Where the faded moon Made a dim silver twilight. Keats.
In a faded manner.A dull room fadedly furnished. Dickens.
Not liable to fade; unfading.
Father. [Obs.] Chaucer.
To fit; to suit; to agree.They shall be made, spite of antipathy, to fadge together. Milton.Well, Sir, how fadges the new design Wycherley.
Losing freshness, color, brightness, or vigor.-- n.
A fathom. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Faded. [R.] Shenstone.
See Fecal.
Excrement; ordure; also, settlings; sediment after infusion ordistillation. [Written also feces.]
See Fecula.
Fairy. [Archaic] Spenser.
To stammer. [Prov. Eng.] Halliwell.
A knot or coarse part in cloth. [Obs.]
Laborious drudgery; esp., the acting as a drudge for another atan English school.
A bassoon. See Fagotto.
The bassoon; -- so called from being divided into parts forease of carriage, making, as it were, a small fagot.
The leaves of an orchid (Angraecum fragrans), of the islands ofBourbon and Mauritius, used (in France) as a substitute for Chinesetea.
A stratum in crystalline rock, containing metallic sulphides.Raymond.
A hydration of iolite.
Conforming to the scale used by Gabriel Daniel Fahrenheit inthe graduation of his thermometer; of or relating to Fahrenheit'sthermometric scale.-- n.
Glazed earthenware; esp., that which is decorated in color.
Fault; failure; omission. [Obs.] Bp. Fell.
A soft silk, heavier than a foulard and not glossy.
With joy; gladly; -- with wold.He would fain have filled his belly with the husks that the swine dideat. Luke xv. 16.Fain Would I woo her, yet I dare not. Shak.
Doing nothing; shiftless.-- n.
A deity recognized as real but conceived as not acting in humanaffairs, hence not worshiped.
The act of fainting, or the state of one who has fainted; aswoon. [R.] See Fainting, n.The saint, Who propped the Virgin in her faint. Sir W. Scott.

Syncope, or loss of consciousness owing to a sudden arrest ofthe blood supply to the brain, the face becoming pallid, therespiration feeble, and the heat's beat weak. Fainting fit, afainting or swoon; syncope. [Colloq.]
Slightly faint; somewhat faint.-- Faint"ish*ness, n.
Timorous; feeble-minded. [Obs.] "A fainting, silly creature."Arbuthnot.
In a faint, weak, or timidmanner.

The impure spirit which comes over first and last in thedistillation of whisky; -- the former being called the strong faints,and the latter, which is much more abundant, the weak faints. Thiscrude spirit is much impregnated with fusel oil. Ure.
Feeble; languid. [R.] Dryden.
Without sudden change of direction or curvature; smooth;fowing; -- said of the figure of a vessel, and of surfaces, waterlines, and other lines.
A catch made by a player on side who makes a prescribed signalthat he will not attempt to advance the ball when caught. He must notthen be interfered with.
Having fair or light-colored hair.
A block, or ring, serving as a guide for the running rigging orfor any rope.
Unprejudiced; just; judicial; honest.-- Fair"*mind`ed*ness, n.
Well-disposed. "A fair-natured prince." Ford.
Using fair speech, or uttered with fairness; bland; civil;courteous; plausible. "A marvelous fair-spoken man." Hooker.
State of prosperity. [Obs.]They think it was never fair-world with them since. Milton.
Fairness; beauty. [Obs.] Foxe.
In the manner of a fairy.Numerous as shadows haunting fairily The brain. Keats.
A present; originally, one given or purchased at a fair. Gay.Fairing box, a box receiving savings or small sums of money. HannahMore.
Tolerably fair. [Colloq.] W. D. Howells.
The state of being fair, or free form spots or stains, as ofthe skin; honesty, as of dealing; candor, as of an argument, etc.
The navigable part of a river, bay, etc., through which vesselsenter or depart; the part of a harbor or channel ehich is kept openand unobstructed for the passage of vessels. Totten. the rough.
The imaginary land or abode of fairies.
Resembling a fairy, or what is made or done be fairies; as,fairylike music.
By my faith; in truth; verily.
Having faith or a faith; honest; sincere. [Obs.] "Make thywords faithed." Shak.
A doer or actor; particularly, an evil doer; a scoundrel.[Obs.]Lo! faitour, there thy meed unto thee take. Spenser.
One of the circles or windings of a cable or hawser, as it liesin a coil; a single turn or coil.
One who fakes something, as a thief, a peddler of petty things,a workman who dresses things up, etc. [Slang]
An Oriental religious ascetic or begging monk. [Written alsofaquir anf fakeer.]
A viverrine mammal of Madagascar (Eupleres Goudotii), allied tothe civet; -- called also Falanouc.
The action of a horse, when he throws himself on his haunchestwo or three times, bending himself, as it were, in very quickcurvets. Harris.
The state of being falcate; a bend in the form of a sickle. SirT. Browne.
One of the mandibles of a spider.
Of or pertaining to Publius Falcidius, a Roman tribune.Falcidian law (Civil Law), a law by which a testator was obliged toleave at least a fourth of his estate to the heir. Burrill.
Having the shape of a scithe or sickle; resembling a reapinghook; as, the falciform ligatment of the liver.
An ancient form of cannon. Chanting falcon. (Zoöl.) See underChanting.
A person who breeds or trains hawks for taking birds or game;one who follows the sport of fowling with hawks. Johnson.
The female or young of the goshawk (Astur palumbarius).
Like a falcon or hawk; belonging to the Falconid�
A curved and sharp-pointed claw.
Curved and sharppointed, like a falcula, or claw of a falcon.
A privilege of setting up, and moving about, folds for sheep,in any fields within manors, in order to manure them; -- oftenreserved to himself by the lord of the manor. Spelman.
A fee or rent paid by a tenant for the privilege of faldage onhis own ground. Blount.
A frieze or rough-napped cloth. [Obs.]
The throne or seat of a bishop within the chancel. [Obs.]
A folding stool, or portable seat, made to fold up in themanner of a camo stool. It was formerly placed in the choir for abishop, when he offciated in any but his own cathedral church.Fairholt.
Of or pertaining to Mount Falernus, in Italy; as,Falernianwine.
The razorbill. [Written also falc, and faik.] [Prov. Eng.]
Embodying or pertaining to a fallacy; illogical; fitted todeceive; misleading; delusive; as, fallacious arguments or reasoning.-- Fal*la"cious*ly, adv. -Fal*la"cious*ness, n.
An argument, or apparent argument, which professes to bedecisive of the matter at issue, while in reality it is not; asophism.
Cavillation; a caviling. [Obs.] Cranmer.
Dropped; prostrate; degraded; ruined; decreased; dead.Some ruined temple or fallen monument. Rogers.
An exception. [Obs.] Jer. Taylor.
A part which acts by falling, as a stamp in a fulling mill, orthe device in a spinning machine to arrest motion when a threadbreaks.
A fresh-water fish of the United States (Semotilus bullaris); -- called also silver chub, and Shiner. The name is also applied toother allied species.
The state of being fallible; liability to deceive or to bedeceived; as, the fallibity of an argument or of an adviser.
Liable to fail, mistake, or err; liable to deceive or to bedeceived; as, all men are fallible; our opinions and hopes arefallible.
In a fallible manner.

from Fall, v. i. Falling away, Falling off, etc. See To fallaway, To fall off, etc., under Fall, v. i.-- Falling band, the plain, broad, linen collar turning down overthe doublet, worn in the early part of the 17th century.-- Falling sickness (Med.), epilepsy. Shak.-- Falling star. (Astron.) See Shooting star.-- Falling stone, a stone falling through the atmosphere; ameteorite; an aërolite.-- Falling tide, the ebb tide.-- Falling weather, a rainy season. [Colloq.] Bartlett.
Pertaining to, or discovered by, Fallopius; as, the Fallopiantubes or oviducts, the ducts or canals which conduct the ova from theovaries to the uterus.
Left untilled or unsowed after plowing; uncultivated; as,fallow ground. Fallow chat, Fallow finch (Zoöl.), a small Europeanbird, the wheatear (Saxicola ænanthe). See Wheatear.
A European species of deer (Cervus dama), much smaller than thered deer. In summer both sexes are spotted with white. It is commonin England, where it is often domesticated in the parks.
One who favors the practice of fallowing land. [R.] Sinclair.
A well or opening, through the successive floors of a warehouseor manufactory, through which goods are raised or lowered. [U.S.]Bartlett.
A falsifier of evidence. [Obs.] Sheldon.

Not in tune. False arch (Arch.), a member having the appearanceof an arch, though not of arch construction.-- False attic, an architectural erection above the main cornice,concealing a roof, but not having windows or inclosing rooms.-- False bearing, any bearing which is not directly upon a verticalsupport; thus, the weight carried by a corbel has a false bearing.-- False cadence, an imperfect or interrupted cadence.-- False conception (Med.), an abnormal conception in which a mole,or misshapen fleshy mass, is produced instead of a properly organizedfetus.-- False croup (Med.), a spasmodic affection of the larynx attendedwith the symptoms of membranous croup, but unassociated with thedeposit of a fibrinous membrane.-- False door or window (Arch.), the representation of a door orwindow, inserted to complete a series of doors or windows or to givesymmetry.-- False fire, a combustible carried by vessels of war, chiefly forsignaling, but sometimes burned for the purpose of deceiving anenemy; also, a light on shore for decoying a vessel to destruction.-- False galena. See Blende.-- False imprisonment (Law), the arrest and imprisonment of a personwithout warrant or cause, or contrary to law; or the unlawfuldetaining of a person in custody.-- False keel (Naut.), the timber below the main keel, used to serveboth as a protection and to increase the shio's lateral resistance.-- False key, a picklock.-- False leg. (Zoöl.) See Proleg.-- False membrane (Med.), the fibrinous deposit formed in croup anddiphtheria, and resembling in appearance an animal membrane.-- False papers (Naut.), documents carried by a ship giving falserepresentations respecting her cargo, destination, ect., for thepurpose of deceiving.-- False passage (Surg.), an unnatural passage leading off from anatural canal, such as the urethra, and produced usually by theunskillful introduction of instruments.-- False personation (Law), the intentional false assumption of thename and personality of another.-- False pretenses (Law), false representations concerning past orpresent facts and events, for the purpose of defrauding another.-- False rail (Naut.), a thin piece of timber placed on top of thehead rail to strengthen it.-- False relation (Mus.), a progression in harmony, in which acertain note in a chord appears in the next chord prefixed by a flator sharp.-- False return (Law), an untrue return made to a process by theofficer to whom it was delivered for execution.-- False ribs (Anat.), the asternal rebs, of which there are fivepairs in man.-- False roof (Arch.), the space between the upper ceiling and theroof. Oxford Gloss.-- False token, a false mark or other symbol, used for fraudulentpurposes.-- False scorpion (Zoöl.), any arachnid of the genus Chelifer. SeeBook scorpion.-- False tack (Naut.), a coming up into the wind and filling awayagain on the same tack.-- False vampire (Zoöl.), the Vampyrus spectrum of South America,formerly erroneously supposed to have blood-sucking habits; -- calledalso vampire, and ghost vampire. The genuine blood-sucking batsbelong to the genera Desmodus and Diphylla. See Vampire.-- False window. (Arch.) See False door, above.-- False wing. (Zoöl.) See Alula, and Bastard wing, under Bastard.-- False works (Civil Engin.), construction works to facilitate theerection of the main work, as scaffolding, bridge centering, etc.
Hypocritical. Shak.
False-hearted. Shak.
Hollow or unsound at the core; treacherous; deceitful;perfidious. Bacon.-- False"*heart`ed*ness, n. Bp. Stillingfleet.

In a false manner; erroneously; not truly; perfidiously ortreacherously. "O falsely, falsely murdered." Shak.Oppositions of science, falsely so called. 1 Tim. vi. 20.Will ye steal, murder . . . and swear falsely Jer. vii. 9.

The state of being false; contrariety to the fact; inaccuracy;want of integrity or uprightness; double dealing; unfaithfulness;treachery; perfidy; as, the falseness of a report, a drawing, or asinger's notes; the falseness of a man, or of his word.
A deceiver. [Obs.] Spenser.
A false or artificial voice; that voice in a man which liesabove his natural voice; the male counter tenor or alto voice. SeeHead voice, under Voice.
The crime of falsifying.
Capable of being falsified, counterfeited, or corrupted.Johnson.
The showing an item of charge in an account to be wrong. Story.
A falsifier. Bp. Morton.
One who falsifies, or gives to a thing a deceptive appearance;a liar.
To avoid or defeat; to prove false, as a judgment. Blackstone.
That which is evidently false; an assertion or statement thefalsity of which is plainly apparent; -- opposed to truism.
To thrash in the chaff; also, to cleanse or sift, as barley.[Prov. Eng.] Halliwell.
Hesitating; trembling. "With faltering speech." Milton.-- n.
A series of strata, of the Middle Tertiary period, of France,abounding in shells, and used by Lyell as the type of his Miocenesubdivision.
Fallow. [Obs.] Chaucer.
A curved fold or process of the dura mater or the peritoneum;esp., one of the partitionlike folds of the dura mater which extendinto the great fissures of the brain.
To stammer. [Obs.] Nares.
Without fame or renown.-- Fame"less*ly, adv.
A confidential officer employed in the service of the tribunal,especially in apprehending and imprisoning the accused.
The act or process of making familiar; the result of becomingfamiliar; as, familiarization with scenes of blood.
In a familiar manner.
Familiarity. [R.]
Of or pertaining to a family or household; domestic. [Obs.]Milton.
The tenets of the Familists. Milton.
One of afanatical Antinomian sect originating in Holland, andexisting in England about 1580, called the Family of Love, who heldthat religion consists wholly in love.
A community in which many persons unite as in one family, andare regulated by certain communistic laws and customs.

A groupe of organisms, either animal or vegetable, related bycertain points of resemblance in structure or development, morecomprehensive than a genus, because it is usually based on fewer orless pronounced points of likeness. In zoölogy a family is lesscomprehesive than an order; in botany it is often considered the samething as an order. Family circle. See under Circle.-- Family man. (a) A man who has a family; esp., one who has a wifeand children living with him andd dependent upon him. (b) A man ofdomestic habits. "The Jews are generally, when married, mostexemplary family men." Mayhew.-- Family of curves or surfaces (Geom.), a group of curves orsurfaces derived from a single equation.-- In a family way, like one belonging to the family. "Why don't weask him and his ladies to come over in a family way, and dine withsome other plain country gentlefolks" Thackeray.-- In the family way, pregnant. [Colloq.]
General scarcity of food; dearth; a want of provisions;destitution. "Worn with famine." Milton.There was a famine in the land. Gen. xxvi. 1.Famine fever (Med.), typhus fever.
State of being famished.
The state or quality of being famous. [Obs.] Johnson.

Celebrated in fame or public report; renowned; mach talked of;distinguished in story; -- used in either a good or a bad sense,chiefly the former; often followed by for; as, famous for erudition,for eloquence, for military skill; a famous pirate.Famous for a scolding tongue. Shak.
Renowned. [Obs.] Shak.
In a famous manner; in a distinguished degree; greatly;splendidly.Then this land was famously enriched With politic grave counsel.Shak.
The state of being famous.
Domestic; familiar. [Obs.] Chaucer.
To serve. [Obs.]
A collegian of inferior rank or position, corresponding to thesizar at Cambridge. [Oxford Univ., Eng.]

Any palm tree having fan-shaped or radiate leaves; as theChamærops humilis of Southern Europe; the species of Sabal andThrinax in the West Indies, Florida, etc.; and especially the greattalipot tree (Corypha umbraculifera) of Ceylon and Malaya. The leavesof the latter are often eighteen feet long and fourteen wide, and areused for umbrellas, tents, and roofs. When cut up, they are used forbooks and manuscripts.
Having the nerves or veins arranged in a radiating manner; --said of certain leaves, and of the winfs of some insects.
Having an expanded, or fan-shaped, tail; as, the fan-tailedpigeon.
A lighthouse, or the apparatus placed in it for giving light.

Pertaining to, or indicating, fanaticism; extravagant inopinions; ultra; unreasonable; excessively enthusiastic, especiallyon religious subjects; as, fanatic zeal; fanatic notions.But Faith, fanatic Faith, once wedded fast To some dear falsehood,hugs it to the last. T. Moore.
Characteristic of, or relating to, fanaticism; fanatic. -Fa*nat"ic*al*ly, adv.-- Fa*nat"ic*al*ness, n.
Excessive enthusiasm, unreasoning zeal, or wild and extravagantnotions, on any subject, especially religion; religious frenzy.
To cause to become a fanatic.
Fanaticism. [R.] Gibbon.
Formed or conceived by the fancy; unreal; as, a fancied wrong.
Having no fancy; without ideas or imagination. [R.]A pert or bluff important wight, Whose brain is fanciless, whoseblood is white. Armstrong.
Free from the power of love. "In maiden meditation, fancy-free." Shak.
Love-sick. Shak.
A lovemonger; a whimsical lover. [Obs.] Shak.
Ornamental work with a needle or hook, as embroidery,crocheting, netting, etc.
imp. of Find. Spenser.
A temple; a place consecrated to religion; a church. [Poet.]Such to this British Isle, her Christian fanes. Wordsworth.
A dry measure in Spain and Spanish America, varying from 1 DeColange.

A flourish of trumpets, as in coming into the lists, etc.;also, a short and lively air performed on hunting horns during thechase.The fanfare announcing the arrival of the various Christian princes.Sir W. Scott.
A bully; a hector; a swaggerer; an empty boaster. [R.] Dryden.
A swaggering; vain boasting; ostentation; a bluster. Swift.

The tusk of an animal, by which the prey is seized and held ortorn; a long pointed tooth; esp., one of the usually erectile,venomous teeth of serpents. Also, one of the falcers of a spider.Since I am a dog, beware my fangs. Shak.
Having fangs or tusks; as, a fanged adder. Also usedfiguratively.
Something new-fashioned; a foolish innovation; a gewgaw; atrifling ornament.
New made; hence, gaudy; showy; vainly decorated. [Obs., exceptwith the prefix new.] See Newfangled. "Our fangled world." Shak.
Quality of being fangled. [Obs.]He them in new fangleness did pass. Spenser.
Destitute of fangs or tusks. "A fangless lion." Shak.
A quantity of wares, as raw silk, etc., from one hundredweight.
A small flag sometimes carried at the head of the baggage of abrigade. [Obs.]
Resembling a fan; -- specifically (Bot.), folded up like a fan,as certain leaves; plicate.
Same as Fanon.
A term applied to various articles, as: (a) A peculiar stripedscarf worn by the pope at mass, and by eastern bishops. (b) Amaniple. [Written also fannel, phanon, etc.]
A continuous composition, not divided into what are calledmovements, or governed by the ordinary rules of musical design, butin which the author's fancy roves unrestricted by set form.
Filled with fancies or imaginations. [Obs.] Shak.
Same as Phantasm.
One whose manners or ideas are fantastic. [R.] Coleridge.
A person given to fantastic dress, manners, etc.; an eccentricperson; a fop. Milton.Our fantastics, who, having a fine watch, take all ocasions to drowit out to be seen. Fuller.
The quality of being fantastic.
Fanciful; unreal; whimsical; capricious; fantastic.
Fantastically. [Obs.]
In a fantastic manner.the letter A, in scarlet, fantastically embroidered with gold thread,upon her bosom. Hawthorne.
The quality of being fantastical; fancifulness; whimsicality.Ruskin.
Fantastically. [Obs.]
Fantasticalness. [Obs.]
A fantastic. [Obs.] Shak.
To have a fancy for; to be pleased with; to like; to fancy.[Obs.] Cavendish.Which he doth most fantasy. Robynson (More's Utopia).
Puppets caused to perform evolutions or dramatic scenes bymeans of machinery; also, the representations in which they are used.
See Phantom. Fantom corn, phantom corn. Grose.
Fuddled. [Obs.] Shak.
See Fakir.
A young pig, or a litter of pigs.
A going out of the way; a digression. [Obs.] Fuller.
Remote; as, the far-off distance. Cf. Far-off, under Far, adv.
Stretched beyond ordinary limits.

The standard unit of electrical capacity; the capacity of acondenser whose charge, having an electro-motive force of one volt,is equal to the amount of electricity which, with the sameelectromotive force, passes through one ohm in one second; thecapacity, which, charged with one coulomb, gives an electro-motiveforce of one volt.

Of or pertaining to Michael Faraday, the distinguishedelectrician; -- applied especially to induced currents ofelectricity, as produced by certain forms of inductive apparatus, onaccount of Faraday's investigations of their laws.
To stimulate with, or subject to, faradic, or inducted,electric currents. --Far"a*diz`er (#), n.
See Farrand, n.
A fabrik made of silk and wool or hair. Simmonds.
A rapid dance in six-eight time in which a large number joinhands and dance in various figures, sometimes moving from room toroom. It originated in Provence.
Orderly; comely; respectable. [Obs.] Halliwell.
Stuffing, or mixture of viands, like that used on dressing afowl; forcemeat.
Stuffing; forcemeat. [Obs.]They spoil a good dish with . . . unsavory farcements. Feltham.

a common species of fern with large decompound fronds(Asplenium Filixfæmina), growing in many countries; lady fern.
double rhymes, or rhymes (called in French feminine rhymesbecause they end in e weak, or feminine) in which two syllables, anaccented and an unaccented one, correspond at the end of each line.

To make, or to describe as, female or feminine. Shaftesbury.

SeeCovert, a., 3.-- Feme sole (Law), a single or unmarried woman; a woman who hasnever been married, or who has been divorced, or whose husband isdead.-- Feme sole trader or merchant (Eng. Law), a married woman, by thecustom of London, engages in business on her own account, inpendentlyof her husband.

A lantern, or louver covering, placed on a roof, forventilation or escape of smoke.
Feminine. [Obs.] West.
Feminity.

In a feminine manner. Byron.
The quality of being feminine; womanliness; womanishness.

Pertaining to the femur or thigh; as, the femoral artery."Femoral habiliments." Sir W. Scott.
Low land overflowed, or covered wholly or partially with water,but producing sedge, coarse grasses, or other aquatic plants; boggyland; moor; marsh.'Mid reedy fens wide spread. Wordsworth.
The mole cricket. [Prov. Eng.]
Sucked out of marches. "Fen-sucked fogs." Shak.
A projection on the bolt, which passes through the tumblergates in locking and unlocking.

the month in which female deer are fawning, when hunting isprohibited. Bullokar.-- Fence roof, a covering for defense. "They fitted their shieldsclose to one another in manner of a fence roof." Holland. [Colloq.]
Affording defense; defensive. [Obs.] Congreve.
Without a fence; uninclosed; open; unguarded; defenseless.Milton.
One who fences; one who teaches or practices the art of fencingwith sword or foil.As blunt as the fencer's foils. Shak.
Capable of being defended, or of making or affording defense.[Obs.]No fort so fencible, nor walls so strong. Spenser.
A soldier enlisted for home service only; -- usually in the pl.
A fiend. [Obs.] Chaucer.

One who or that which defends or protects by warding off harm;as:(a) A screen to prevent coals or sparks of an open fire from escapingto the floor.(b) Anything serving as a cushion to lessen the shock when a vesselcomes in contact with another vessel or a wharf.(c) A screen to protect a carriage from mud thrown off the wheels:also, a splashboard.(d) Anything set up to protect an exposed angle, as of a house, fromdamage by carriage wheels.
Fiendlike. [Obs.] Chaucer.
To put money to usury; to lend on interest. [Obs.] Cockeram.
The act of fenerating; interest. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.
Any small windowlike opening or recess, esp. one to show therelics within an altar, or the like.

Pertaining to a window or to windows.
Having transparent spots, as the wings of certain butterflies.

One of the openings in a fenestrated structure.

A pheasantlike bird of rich plumage and graceful form andmovement, fabled to appear in the land on the accession of a sage tothe throne, or when right principles are about to prevail. It isoften represented on porcelains and other works of art.

A system of spirit influences for good and evil believed by theChinese to attend the natural features of landscape; also, a kind ofgeomancy dealing with these influences, used in determining sites forgraves, houses, etc.
A kind of marble or alabaster, sometimes used for windows onaccount of its transparency.

The principles, purposes, and methods of the Fenians.
The refuse whale blubber, used as a manure, and in themanufacture of Prussian blue. Ure.
A small, African, foxlike animal (Vulpes zerda) of a pale fawncolor, remarkable for the large size of its ears.

Milton.A sprig of fennel was in fact the theological smelling bottle of thetender sex. S. G. Goodrich.Azorean, or Sweet, fennel, (Fæniculum dulce). N.Damascenais common in gardens. N.sativa furnishes the fennel seed, used as acondiment, etc., in India. These seeds are the "fitches" mentioned inIsaiah (xxviii. 25).-- Fennel water (Med.), the distilled water of fennel seed. Abounding in fens; fenny.
Pertaining to, or inhabiting, a fen; abounding in fens; swampy;boggy. "Fenny snake." Shak.
Corrupted; decayed; moldy. See Vinnewed. [Obs.] Dr. Favour.
Fencible. [Obs.] Spenser.

A plant (trigonella Foenum Græcum) cultivated for its strong-smelling seeds, which are "now only used for giving false importanceto horse medicine and damaged hay." J. Smith (Pop. Names of Plants,1881).
A feud. See 2d Feud. Blackstone.
Feudal. See Feudal.
Feudal tenure; the feudal system. See Feudality. Burke.

, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Feoffed; p. pr. & vb. n.. Feoffing.]Etym: [OE. feffen, OF. feffer, fieffer, F. fieffer, fr. fief fief;cf. LL. feoffare, fefare. See Fief.] (Law)

One who enfeoffs or grants a fee.
Far. [Obs.] Chaucer.
A large, venomous serpent (Trigonocephalus lanceolatus) ofBrazil and the West Indies. It is allied to the rattlesnake, but hasno rattle.
Fruitful; producing abudantly. [R.] Thomson.
The state of being feracious or fruitful. [Obs.] Beattie.
A group of mammals which formerly included the Carnivora,Insectivora, Marsupialia, and lemurs, but is now often restricted tothe Carnivora.
Of a wild nature; -- applied to animals, as foxes, wild ducks,etc., in which no one can claim property.
Wild; untamed; ferine; not domesticated; -- said of beasts,birds, and plants. feral child, not raised by humans

A measure of land mentioned in Domesday Book. It is supposed tohave consisted of a few acres only. [Obs.]
Fearfulness. [Obs.] Chaucer.
A mate or companion; -- often used of a wife. [Obs.] [Writtenalso fear and feere.] Chaucer.And Cambel took Cambrina to his fere. Spenser.In fere, together; in company. [Obs.] Chaucer.
A portable bier or shrine, variously adorned, used forcontaining relics of saints. Mollett.
Far forth. [Obs.] As ferforth as, as far as.-- So ferforth, to such a degree.
Ferforth. [Obs.] Chaucer.
A mineral of a brownish black color, essentially a tantalo-niobate of yttrium, erbium, and cerium; -- so called after RobertFerguson.
A week day, esp. a day which is neither a festival nor a fast.Shipley.
Same as Feria.
The act of keeping holiday; cessation from work. [Obs.] Sir T.Browne.
A holiday. [Obs.] Bullokar.
, compar. of Fere, fierce. [Obs.]Rhenus ferier than the cataract. Marston.
Wild; untamed; savage; as, lions, tigers, wolves, and bears areferine beasts. Sir M. Hale.-- n.
The name given to Europeans by the Hindos. [Written alsoFeringhee.]
Wildness; savageness; fierceness. [Obs.] Woodward.
Singular; wonderful; extraordinary. [Obs.] -- n.
Medicine; pharmacy. [Obs.] Chaucer.
To cause ferment of fermentation in; to set in motion; toexcite internal emotion in; to heat.Ye vigorous swains! while youth ferments your blood. Pope.

Capable of fermentation; as, cider and other vegetable liquorsare fermentable.
Fermentative. [Obs.]

Causing, or having power to cause, fermentation; produced byfermentation; fermenting; as, a fermentative process.-- Fer*ment"a*tive*ly, adv.-- Fer*ment"a*tive*ness, n.
The officer in a religious house who had the care of theinfirmary. [Obs.]
The mechanism for closing the breech of a breech-loadingfirearm, in artillery consisting principally of the breechblock,obturator, and carrier ring.

Long ago. [Obs.] Chaucer.

Abounding in ferns.

A symbol of the solar deity, found on monuments exhumed inBabylon, Nineveh, etc.
Wild; savage. [R.] Arthur Wilson.
A stuff made of silk and wool.I did buy a colored silk ferrandine. Pepys.

An increase in the ratio of transformation of an alternatingcurrent converter, accompanied by other changes in electricalconditions, occurring when the secondary of the converter isconnected with a condenser of moderate capacity; -- so called becausefirst observed in connection with the Ferranti cables in London.
A sword bearing the mark of one of the Ferrara family of Italy.These swords were highly esteemed in England and Scotland in the 16thand 17th centuries.
Pertaining to Ferrara, in Italy.-- n., sing. & pl.
The art of working in iron. [Obs.] Chapman.
A salt of ferric acid.
Partaking of, made of, or pertaining to, iron; like iron.[Obs.] Sir T. Browne.
superl. of Fer. Chaucer.

One who ferrets. Johnson.
Copper sulphide, used to color glass. Hebert.
A combining form indicating ferric iron as an ingredient; as,ferricyanide.
The price or fare to be paid for passage at a ferry.

Pertaining to, derived from, or containing iron. Specifically(Chem.), denoting those compounds in which iron has a higher valencethan in the ferrous compounds; as, ferric oxide; ferric acid. A salt of ferricyanic acid; a ferricyanide.

One of a complex series of double cyanides of ferric iron andsome other base. Producing or yielding iron.
A ferricyanate; a ferricyanide. [R.]

G.Ferris, American engineer, who erected the first of its kind for theWorld's Columbian Exposition in Chicago in 1893.
A prefix, or combining form, indicating ferrous iron as aningredient; as, ferrocyanide.

Concrete strengthened by a core or foundation skeleton of ironor steel bars, strips, etc. Floors, columns, piles, water pipes,etc., have been successfully made of it. Called also armored concretesteel, and reënforced concrete.
Limestone containing a large percentage of iron carbonate, andhence turning brown on exposure.
A salt of ferrocyanic acid; a ferrocyanide.

Pertaining to, derived from, or designating, a ferrocyanide.ferrocyanic acid (Chem.), a white crystalline substance, H4(CN)6Fe,of strong acid properties, obtained from potassium ferrocyanide, andregarded as the type of the ferrocyanides; -- called also hydro-ferrocyanic acid, hydrogen ferrocyanide. etc.

One of a series of complex double cyanides of ferrous iron andsome other base. Potassium ferrocyanide (Chem.), yellow prussiate ofpotash; a tough, yellow, crystalline salt, K4(CN)6Fe, the startingpoint in the manufacture of almost all cyanogen compounds, and thebasis of the ferric ferrocyanate, prussian blue. It is obtained bystrongly heating together potash, scrap iron, and animal mattercontaining nitrogen, as horn, leather, blood, etc., in iron pots.
A ferrocyanate; a ferocyanide. [R.]
Ferrocyanic.

A photographic picture taken on an iron plate by a collodionprocess; -- familiarly called tintype.
Pertaining to, or derived from, iron; -- especially used ofcompounds of iron in which the iron has its lower valence; as,ferrous sulphate.
Having the color or properties of the rust of iron.
Ferruginous. [R.]
A disease of plants caused by fungi, commonly called the rust,from its resemblance to iron rust in color.

Fourth. [Obs.] Chaucer.

The state or quality of being fertile or fruitful;fruitfulness; productiveness; fecundity; richness; abundance ofresources; fertile invention; quickness; readiness; as, the fertilityof soil, or of imagination. "fertility of resource." E. Everett.And all her husbandry doth lie on heaps Corrupting in its ownfertility. Shak.Thy very weeds are beautiful; thy waste More rich than other climes'fertility. Byron.

The act of fecundating or impregnating animal or vegetablegerms; esp., the process by which in flowers the pollen renders theovule fertile, or an analogous process in flowerless plants;fecundation; impregnation. Close fertilization (Bot.), thefertilization of pistils by pollen derived from the stamens of thesame blossom.-- Cross fertilization, fertilization by pollen from some otherblossom. See under Cross, a.
Pertaining to reeds and canes; having a stalk like a reed; as,ferulaceous plants.

A flat piece of wood, used for striking, children, esp. on thehand, in punishment.
Pertaining to, or derived from, asafetida (Ferula asafoetida);as, ferulic acid. [Written also ferulaic.]
Heat; fervency. [Obs.]
The state of being fervent or warm; ardor; warmth of feeling ordevotion; eagerness.When you pray, let it be with attention, with fervency, and withperseverance. Wake.
Growing hot.
Pertaining to, or resembling, the Fescennines.-- n.
A grass of the genus Festuca. Fescue grass (Bot.), a genus ofgrasses (Festuca) containing several species of importance inagriculture. Festuca ovina is sheep's fescue; F. elatior is meadowfescue.
See Phasel. [Obs.] May (Georgics).
Weariness. [Obs.] Bailey.
In the manner of fess.

To feast; to entertain. [Obs.] Chaucer.
A time of feasting or celebration; an anniversary day of joy,civil or religious.The morning trumpets festival proclaimed. Milton.
Hasty; hurried. [Obs.] -- Fes"ti*nate*ly, adv. [Obs.] Shak.
Haste; hurry. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.
Pertaining to a fest; festive; festal; appropriate to afestival; joyous; mirthful.I cannot woo in festival terms. Shak.
Pertaining to, or becoming, a feast; festal; joyous; gay;mirthful; sportive.-- Fes"tive*ly, adv.The glad circle round them yield their souls To festive mirth and witthat knows no gall. Thomson.
Pertaining to a feast; festive. [R.] Sir W. Scott.
Festive; fond of festive occasions. [Obs.] "A festlich man."Chaucer.
A carved ornament consisting of flowers, and leaves, intermixedor twisted together, wound with a ribbon, and hanging or depending ina natural curve. See Illust. of Bucranium.
Pertaining to, consisting of, or resembling, festoons. Sir J.Herschel.
Of a straw color; greenish yellow. [Obs.]A little insect of a festucine or pale green. Sir T. Browne.
Formed or consisting of straw. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

Pertaining to, or connected with, a fetus; as, fetalcirculation; fetal membranes.

Neat; feat. [Obs.] Herrick.

The young or embryo of an animal in the womb, or in the egg;often restricted to the later stages in the development of viviparousand oviparous animals, embryo being applied to the earlier stages.[Written also foetus.]

To set close; to fix in rest, as a spear. Spenser.
A dog keeper. [Obs.] Massinger.

A slight fever. [Obs.] Ayliffe.
A perennial plant (Pyrethrum, or Chrysanthemum, Parthenium)allied to camomile, having finely divided leaves and white blossoms;-- so named from its supposed febrifugal qualities.
Feverishly. [Obs.] Donne.

Feverish. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

Not many; small, limited, or confined in number; -- indicatinga small portion of units or individuals constituing a whole; often,by ellipsis of a noun, a few people. "Are not my days few" Job x. 20.Few know and fewer care. Proverb.

Fated; doomed. [Old Eng. & Scot.]
To feign. [Obs.] Chaucer.
A fair or market. [Obs.] Chaucer.
A felt or cloth cap, usually red and having a tassel, -- avariety of the tarboosh. See Tarboosh. B. Taylor.
A kind of French hackney coach.
To betroth; to affiance. [Obs.] Harmar.
A betrothed woman.
The dung of the fox, wolf, boar, or badger.

Commission; fiat; order; decree. [Obs.] Spenser.
A falsehood; a lie; -- used euphemistically.They are very serious; they don't tell fibs. H. James.
One who tells fibs.
Having the form of a fiber or fibers; resembling a fiber.

An order of sponges having a fibrous skeleton, including thecommercial sponges.
Containing, or consisting of, fibers; as, the fibrous coat ofthe cocoanut; the fibrous roots of grasses.-- Fi"brous*ness, n.
Containing woody fiber and ducts, as the stems of all floweringplants and ferns; -- opposed to cellular.
One who tells fibs. [Jocular]
Pertaining to the fibula.
The outer and usually the smaller of the two bones of the leg,or hind limb, below the knee.

A small dog; -- written also fise, fyce, fiste, etc. [SouthernU.S.]
